title: Dennis Davis (drummer) - Wikipedia
notes: Born 28 August 1951, Manhattan; died of cancer 6 April 2016. Studied with Max Roach and Elvin Jones before joining the Clark Terry Big Band in 1967; US Navy 1969-70 (USS Rowan), the Navy's Drum and Bugle Corps. Met Carlos Alomar in Roy Ayers's band; hired by Bowie in 1974 for two Young Americans tracks; Alomar, Davis and George Murray, the 'D.A.M. Trio', on seven successive Bowie albums of the 1970s and three live albums. 'The snare sound used on Bowie's Low album is considered influential on many later records. It was the result of early pitch shifting technology coupled with Davis's sensitive touch as a performer.' Four albums with Stevie Wonder over the next decade (Hotter than July's Master Blaster among them); percussion on Bowie's tours in the early 2000s, with his former student Sterling Campbell on drums. Tony Visconti, in his son Hikaru's interview videos, on his Look Back in Anger drum and conga tracks: he 'plays so many things at once... and yet it doesn't sound busy'. Roy Ayers from Red, Black and Green (1973) to Mahogany Vibe (2004).

title: Young Americans (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, 1975. Davis on the two Electric Lady tracks of January 1975, Fame and Across the Universe, with John Lennon and Harry Maslin; the Sigma Sound tracks are Andy Newmark's.

title: Fame (David Bowie song) - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, Lennon and Alomar, 1975; US number one. Personnel: Dennis Davis, drums and vibraslap; Emir Ksasan, bass; Alomar and Earl Slick, guitars; Lennon, backing vocals and guitar. A funk, funk-rock and soul song.

title: Station to Station - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, 1976, recorded at Cherokee, Los Angeles, late 1975, co-produced with Harry Maslin. 'The sessions established the lineup of guitarist Carlos Alomar, bassist George Murray and drummer Dennis Davis that Bowie would use for the rest of the decade.' Davis: drums, and percussion on 1-3 and 5.

title: Station to Station (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Over ten minutes: a slow march (6/4 against 4/4 per the article) until 'a thud of drums signals a change of tempo and key and the band erupts into what Alan Light of Rolling Stone calls a "celebratory groove"'. Bowie credits Neu! and Klaus Dinger's 'almost-but-not-quite robotic/machine drumming'.

title: TVC 15 - Wikipedia
notes: Station to Station, 1976: Davis on drums; the same team as Fame.

title: Low (David Bowie album) - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, 1977, mostly at the Château d'Hérouville from 1 September 1976. 'Drum sound': Davis's snare processed by Tony Visconti through an Eventide H910 Harmonizer, fed back into itself for 'an infinite dropping of [the] pitch'; Buckley calls it 'brutal', 'mechanistic', 'revolutionary', especially on Speed of Life, Breaking Glass and Sound and Vision; Davis said it sounded 'as big as a house'; Rob Sheffield, 'one of rock's all-time most imitated drum sounds'. Stephen Morris asked Joy Division's engineer for the drums of Speed of Life on An Ideal for Living (1978). Davis was the sessions' 'comedian'.

title: Sound and Vision - Wikipedia
notes: Low's single. Davis thought it sounded 'like a Crusaders tune'; Murray heard Bo Diddley; the drums through the Harmonizer at Visconti's insistence. Personnel: Dennis Davis, drums.

title: "Heroes" (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, 1977, Hansa, West Berlin; Alomar, Murray and Davis the core band, with Robert Fripp and Brian Eno. Davis: drums, percussion.

title: "Heroes" (David Bowie song) - Wikipedia
notes: The backing track: Bowie on piano, Alomar, Murray and Davis, who with Murray provided the 'hypnotic pulse'. Visconti 'buried Davis's kick drum, finding the track "more energetic without it"'. 'The song is led by Davis's drum beat', 'a steadfast marker of rock and roll rhythm ... faded way back in the mix' (Tiffany Naiman); Feldner compares it to krautrock's 'motoric' beat.

title: Lodger (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, 1979, Mountain Studios, Montreux, and the Record Plant. Davis: drums on 1, 4-6, 9 and 10; percussion on 2, 3 and 7; bass guitar on 8 (Boys Keep Swinging), where Carlos Alomar plays the drums. Oblique Strategies; the band swapped instruments.

title: Scary Monsters (and Super Creeps) - Wikipedia
notes: Bowie, 1980, the Power Station, New York, and Good Earth, London. Davis's drums on the title track compared to Stephen Morris's on She's Lost Control: the rhythm section took inspiration from Joy Division.

title: Ashes to Ashes (David Bowie song) - Wikipedia
notes: UK number one, 1980. 'Davis initially struggled with the ska-influenced drumbeat. Bowie played the beat he envisioned for the drummer on a chair and cardboard box, which Davis studied and learned, recording the final take the next day.' Reportedly inspired by Madness's My Girl.

title: Fashion (David Bowie song) - Wikipedia
notes: Scary Monsters, 1980: began as a reggae parody, 'Jamaica'; Davis on drums. Its video's drummer is the Rumour's Stephen Goulding, not Davis.
